Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette: Mohammad is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a hairdresser in a bustling salon. He recently sought help due to the debilitating effects of his PTSD symptoms stemming from a life-threatening illness he experienced several years ago. Mohammad was diagnosed with acute leukemia, and the harrowing experience has left lasting psychological scars. Mohammad’s traumatic memories often resurface through specific triggers that can disrupt his daily functioning. For instance, when he wakes up from nightmares about being in the hospital, the vivid images and sensations flood back instantly, causing a surge of fear and horror. These nightmares are particularly potent because they transport him back to the moment when doctors informed him about the severity of his condition and the dire implications it held. Even mundane activities can trigger intense reactions. For example, a routine medical examination brings on overwhelming physical reactivity; his heart races, and he feels an immediate sense of danger as if he were still in the hospital. The photos from that time—pictures of him hooked up to IVs or lying in a hospital bed—are especially distressing. Each visual cue sets off a cascade of negative emotions and bodily sensations. When Mohammad recalls these experiences, he often smells antiseptic and other medical odors associated with the hospital environment. These olfactory cues trigger both physical pain reminiscent of his ordeal and an intense emotional response without any clear image—just a visceral sense of anguish and helplessness. This combination makes him believe that his body is unreliable, constantly betraying him by reacting as if he were still in danger. Mohammad has come to view his body as the enemy, perpetually tense and on high alert. He feels this tension acutely during moments when he encounters medical-related triggers, which then intensify his negative emotions and physical reactivity. This cycle exacerbates his fear that he is losing control of himself and going crazy, leading him to avoid any situation reminiscent of his illness. His occupation as a hairdresser provides a daily backdrop for these experiences. The sterile smell in the salon sometimes reminds him of hospital environments, causing immediate anxiety and tension. He avoids clients who look ill or request treatments that remind him of medical procedures. This avoidance has strained his professional relationships, leading to fewer appointments and reduced income. The negative appraisals Mohammad holds about his body further reinforce his threat perception. When he feels the emotional intensity without a clear image, it convinces him that his reactions are irrational and a sign of instability. These beliefs then feed back into his triggers, making each encounter with them more fraught and distressing. Mohammad’s memory also plays a critical role in this cycle. When he smells antiseptics or feels pain in certain parts of his body, it reignites his sense of danger and negative emotions. The emotional intensity without clear images further intensifies the threat, making him feel as though he is reliving the trauma. These interconnected experiences have led Mohammad to a point where he recognizes that his life has become unmanageable due to his constant fear and distress. He hopes for relief from these overwhelming feelings and seeks therapy to regain control over his reactions and improve his quality of life. The most pressing concern for Mohammad is the fear that his symptoms will worsen, leading him deeper into a spiral of anxiety and avoidance.
